Fair — that line meant: *ask for three cheap blood tests, not a big expensive package.* Here's the whole thing again in plain words, nothing dropped.

## What you probably have

A condition called **primary palmar hyperhidrosis** — "your hands sweat too much, for no underlying reason." About 1–5% of people have it. Your sweat glands are normal; the nerves that switch them on are just set too high. It's a recognized medical condition with real treatments, not something you have to live around.

"Primary" means nothing else is causing it. "Secondary" would mean some other illness is making you sweat, and the sweating is just the symptom.

## Is anything else causing it?

It's the ordinary "primary" kind if:

- It started when you were a kid or teenager
- Both hands, about equally
- It's your hands (maybe feet, armpits, face too) — not your whole body
- **It stops when you're asleep**
- Someone else in your family has it (very common)

It might be caused by something else if any of these are true:

| What you'd notice | What it could mean |
|---|---|
| It started suddenly as an adult | something else is going on |
| Your whole body sweats, you sweat at night, you're losing weight | overactive thyroid, or something needing a proper check |
| Racing heart, shaky hands, you can't stand heat | overactive thyroid |
| Sweating comes in attacks with headaches and blood pressure spikes | a rare adrenal gland tumour |
| Only one hand, or odd patches | a nerve problem |
| You take antidepressants (SSRIs), opioids, or Alzheimer's medication | the medicine is doing it |

**If any of those apply**, three cheap blood tests answer it: a thyroid test (called TSH), a fasting blood sugar, and a basic blood count (called CBC or "hemogram"). Those three are enough. If a clinic wants to sell you a big bundle of twenty tests for sweaty hands, you don't need it.

## Treatments, cheapest and easiest first

| | Treatment | What it's like |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Strong antiperspirant for hands** (20% aluminium chloride) | Rub it on completely dry hands before bed, wash it off in the morning. Sold over the counter in Turkish pharmacies — Odaban and Perspirex are the usual names. It can make your skin itchy and red, which is why most people give up; start every third night instead of nightly. |
| 2 | **Iontophoresis** — a tray of tap water with a weak electric current | This is the one that fits your problem best. You rest your palms in shallow water for 20–30 minutes while a mild current runs through it. Four times a week to start, then about once a week to keep it up. You buy the machine once (Dermadry, Hidrex, RA Fischer) and use it at home forever. No drugs. It works especially well for hands. |
| 3 | **Pills** (glycopyrrolate or oxybutynin) | These dial down the sweating nerves everywhere in your body. Almost everyone gets a dry mouth. They also make it harder for your body to cool itself, so they're a bad idea in summer heat or when exercising. |
| 4 | **Botox injections in the palms** | Works very well, lasts 4–6 months, then you repeat it. Injections in the palm hurt, so they numb the hand first. Small chance your grip feels weak for a few weeks afterwards. |
| 5 | **Surgery** (cutting the nerve in the chest — "ETS") | Almost always stops the hand sweating, and it cannot be undone. Most people then start sweating heavily on their back and torso instead, and some end up worse off than before. Only after everything above has failed. |

Do 1 and 2 at the same time. That combination is enough for most people, and they never need the rest.

## Which doctor to see

**Go to a dermatologist (dermatoloji).** Skin doctors handle everything from step 1 to step 4, and they'll recognize this immediately.

- A **hormone doctor (endokrinoloji)** only if one of the warning signs above applies, or your thyroid test comes back abnormal.
- A **chest surgeon (göğüs cerrahisi)** only after steps 1–4 have failed. Some hospitals in Turkey run "hiperhidroz" clinics inside the surgery department. If you walk in there first, the whole conversation tilts toward an operation you probably don't need.

## In the meantime

Coffee and nicotine make it worse directly. So does stress — which is why it gets bad exactly when you're concentrating hard on something. You can start the antiperspirant tonight; it's cheap and needs no prescription.

Keep the fan for now. But this is fixable — you shouldn't have to keep it.

column2:
Right about electrocution. Wrong that it makes mistakes harmless — because the injury this device actually causes isn't electrocution, it's burns, and burns aren't bounded by voltage.

## Where you're right

A 3S LiPo boosted to 40 V has no topological path to mains. That's not a mitigation, it's an impossibility, and it removes the only failure mode that would kill you. DC also helps you: for shocks longer than one cardiac cycle, the fibrillation threshold is far above the AC figure — hundreds of mA, not tens. At 40 V you cannot get there through a human.

So the instinct — *make safety a property of the topology rather than of the firmware* — is the correct instinct. It's just that voltage isn't the binding constraint in this particular application.

## Where it breaks

**1. 40 V is above the limit that applies to a body in water.**

The familiar SELV number, 120 V DC, assumes dry intact skin. The standards drop it hard as conditions get wet:

| Condition | SELV limit |
|---|---|
| Dry, general (IEC 61140) | 50 V AC / 120 V DC |
| Damp / wet | as low as 6 V AC |
| **Immersed — Zone 0, pools and baths** | **12 V AC / 30 V DC** |

You are building the immersed case, deliberately: wet hands, large contact area, in salted water. 40 V is outside the regime where "it's low voltage" is an accepted safety argument on its own.

**2. Voltage doesn't bound the injury. Current density does.**

The published ceiling for iontophoresis is **0.5 mA/cm²**. That's the real design number, and your voltage limiter is blind to it.

An immersed palm is roughly 100 cm². 30 mA across it is ~0.3 mA/cm² — fine. The same 30 mA finding a 1 cm² path — a ring you forgot, a hangnail, a knuckle resting against the electrode above the waterline — is 30 mA/cm². Sixty times the limit, at a voltage that never left spec. Current concentration is a geometry failure. No voltage limit sees it.

**3. The dominant injury is chemical, and it's dosed in charge, not volts.**

DC through saline electrolyses it: NaOH accumulates at the cathode, HCl at the anode, both against your skin. That's an alkali and acid burn, and its severity scales with **milliamps × minutes**. It's why clinical DC iontophoresis sessions are capped around 15 minutes.

A perfectly voltage-limited supply that runs 30 mA for three hours because the firmware hung will burn both hands, and every measurement you take during it will read within design limits.

**4. A shorted pass element isn't an over-voltage event.**

If the IRF540N fails short, nothing exceeds 40 V — the rail is the rail. But wet, immersed, hand-to-hand impedance can fall to several hundred ohms. 40 V into 500 Ω is 80 mA: not lethal as DC, but nearly three times your intended dose, delivered instantly, with no ramp. Your voltage limit holds perfectly throughout and does not help.

## The one path your limit sits on the wrong side of

That board has a USB-C port for charging and programming.

If you ever treat while plugged into a cheap non-isolated wall wart, the fault path is charger → board ground → water → you. Your 40 V compliance limit is downstream of that; it constrains the treatment rail, not the charger's insulation. This is the entire reason the reference design carries the Ag7200 and the optocouplers.

**The cheap fix, and I'd do this regardless of whether you keep the isolation:** make charging and treating physically mutually exclusive. Detect VBUS and hold the output relays open, or use a mechanical switch that can't select both. One interlock deletes the whole mains failure class for pennies, and it's easier to verify than an isolation barrier is.

## So the rule isn't "limit the voltage"

It's **three independent hardware limits, none of which the firmware can override**:

| Limit | Bounds | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Voltage | the electrocution case | your 40 V rail — or 30 V if you want to be inside the immersed SELV number |
| **Current** | burns from over-dose and shorted pass elements | the 50 mA fuse in that design; a proper current limit is better |
| **Time** | the electrochemical dose | a hardware one-shot, not a `millis()` check |

Worth knowing about the 30 V option: it puts you inside the immersed limit, but skin impedance is highest at the start of a session, and 30 V may not push 15 mA through it. That tension is exactly why commercial units chose current regulation with 40–50 V of compliance over a fixed low voltage. If you try 30 V, expect a slower ramp-in and test it before committing the layout.

## The printer

Genuinely useful here, in three places.

The STEP files for case and lid are in `3d/CAD/`. PETG or ABS as the repo says — but **do not treat an FDM print as an insulation barrier.** Layer lines are porous, prints wick water, and dielectric performance across a layer boundary is not something you can assume. It's a case, not the thing standing between 40 V and your hand.

The better use is the part the reference design mentions only in passing: **print the non-conductive mesh that holds your palm off the electrode.** A grid sitting a few millimetres above the plate, so your hand is coupled through water across its whole area and can never make direct metal contact. That's the fix for the current-concentration problem in point 2 — the failure mode with no electrical mitigation at all. It's the highest-value thing your printer does for this project.

Print the trays too if you like, but seal them or use glass; you want the vessel watertight for reasons that have nothing to do with electricity.

Sources: [Extra Low Voltage — Electrical Installation Guide (IEC 60364)](https://www.electrical-installation.org/enwiki/Extra_Low_Voltage_(ELV)) · [IEC TS 60479-1 preview — DC fibrillation thresholds](https://webstore.ansi.org/preview-pages/IEC/preview_iec60479-1%7Bed4.1%7Den.pdf) · [Electrical Safety in Iontophoresis — Rehab Management](https://rehabpub.com/clinic-management/regulatory/electrical-safety-in-iontophoresis/) · [Iontophoresis in dermatology — IJDVL](https://ijdvl.com/iontophoresis-in-dermatology/)

`uall` never updates Xcode, and I can see exactly where that breaks, but not why Spotlight behaves this way.

**The chain:**
1. Xcode updates come from the App Store. `uall` covers App Store apps through `mas upgrade`.
2. mas only upgrades apps it finds, and it finds them with a single Spotlight query limited to `/Applications`.
3. That query doesn't return Xcode. So `mas list` doesn't include Xcode, and `mas upgrade` skips it. That's why it's still on 16.2 when 26.3 is current.
4. Every run, mas notices a receipt at `/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/_MASReceipt` without a matching Spotlight result. It prints the warning and runs `mdimport` on Xcode, which changes nothing, so the warning repeats.

**What I compared, Xcode against Pages, which mas does find:**

| | Pages | Xcode |
|---|---|---|
| Found by the `/Applications`-scoped query | yes | **no** |
| Found by a query across all folders | yes | yes |
| App Store ID and receipt in its metadata | yes | yes |
| Recorded path | `/System/Volumes/Data/Applications/…` | same |
| Owner and permissions | root:wheel, 755 | same |
| Date added to the index | 2026-08-27 | same |
| Contents of the bundle indexed | no | no |

Every attribute I can inspect is the same for both. Only the folder-scoped query tells them apart, and macOS has no tool that shows how Spotlight files an entry under a folder. column2:
**Vite is the build tool, not the server.** It belongs in the stack, but only on the frontend side — it never ships to the end user.

Two separate things people conflate:

| | What runs | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **`vite dev`** | Vite's dev server, HMR, on-the-fly transforms | The developer's machine only. Never on the user's. |
| **`vite build`** | Nothing — it emits static `dist/` (hashed JS/CSS/assets) | Those files get embedded in your binary and served by it |

So: Vite yes, `vite dev` in production no. Shipping `npm run dev` to end users drags the whole `node_modules` toolchain onto their machine and is the single most common way these local-server apps end up fragile. `vite preview` is explicitly not a production server either.

## The dev loop

Vite's proxy is what makes this pleasant. In `vite.config.js`:

```js
server: {
  proxy: { '/api': 'http://127.0.0.1:8080' }
}
```

Frontend on 5173 with hot reload, backend on 8080, no CORS, same-origin paths. In production both collapse into one origin because the binary serves `dist/` and `/api` itself — so the frontend code needs no environment switch.

## The one server-side gotcha

If the UI does client-side routing, the binary needs a catch-all that returns `index.html` for any unmatched non-`/api` path. Otherwise a refresh on `/settings` 404s. In Go that's a `http.FileServer` wrapper; in Node, `app.get('*', …)` after the API routes.

Is there a competitor worth considering? Not really — Vite is the default now, and the alternatives (webpack, Parcel) buy nothing here. If the frontend is simple enough to be a couple of hand-written HTML files, skip the build step entirely and serve them directly.

**On the macOS upgrade, the thing that matters most:** you don't need Tahoe. Xcode 27 needs macOS 26.6 or later, and **macOS 27 "Golden Gate"** (released 14 Sep, the `macOS 27` line in your `uall` report) is Apple's answer to exactly the complaints you have about Tahoe.

**How people see Tahoe (macOS 26):** the reaction to Liquid Glass on the Mac was harsh.
- The main complaints are readability: text blending into translucent backgrounds, controls that are hard to tell apart, and inconsistent window corners.
- Developer Simon B. Støvring called it "not so bad" on iPhone and iPad, but "an abomination" on the Mac.
- Apple kept the design anyway; it isn't going away.

**How macOS 27 changes it:**
- A system-wide slider in System Settings, from fully clear glass to fully tinted (close to opaque).
- Less transparency by default, and glass that blurs busy content behind it better.
- The same corner radius on all windows again.
- Six Colors' review is titled "Bridging the Tahoe gap"; reviewers say 27 fixes most of Tahoe's visual problems.
- One caveat: Apple scaled back some of the UI improvements partway through the beta, so some reviewers found the early betas better than the final release.

**If you upgrade and still dislike the look:** System Settings → Accessibility → Display → *Reduce transparency* and *Increase contrast*. Together they come closest to Sequoia's look. On 27, setting the new slider to fully tinted does most of that on its own.

**Also:**
- 27.0 is five days old. I haven't checked early bug reports.
- The upgrade is one-way in practice: going back to Sequoia means erasing the disk and restoring from a backup.

column2:
Yes, but narrowly. The pipeline should learn two things, not a job system: reach an engine by URL, and run one lane on another host. Everything you would want from the Deck falls out of those two.

**Why it fits the code as it stands.** The run command is four steps in sequence, each reading and writing files in a piece's work directory. Status is derived from those files, and lineage is file-based. Engines are reached one of two ways: over HTTP, which is Kokoro and Ollama, or by subprocess, which is ComfyUI's venv, ffmpeg and AutoClip's venv. So the remote question splits cleanly by that distinction.

**Mechanism one: engines by URL.** Kokoro and Ollama are already HTTP services; the only defect is that the address is hardcoded to localhost in `video/short.py`. Replace the port knob with a URL knob in the local config, defaulting to localhost when unset, and the Deck's tailnet name goes there. The existing health probe then reports the remote engine's liveness in the Work tab unchanged. ComfyUI has the same HTTP shape and could take the same knob, but stills stay on this Mac, so it earns nothing today. The value of the pattern is that a rented CUDA box later slots in the same way.

**Mechanism two: a lane on another host.** AutoClip runs in-process under its own venv, so the remote unit is the whole clip command, not a stage inside it. The clip lane gains a host parameter; when set, pipectl wraps the identical command in SSH to the Deck, where the checkout, the venv, Whisper and ffmpeg live. This is the lane worth moving: transcribing a long video is the one step that ties up this Mac for a long time and needs no GPU.

**What makes both work: a shared staging tree.** Because status and lineage are read off files, the Deck's outputs need only land in the same work directory for the Mac to see a finished step. Syncthing on the staging directory does that, and it is the same Syncthing the storage tier already calls for. One rule keeps it safe: a piece is written by the host running it, never both.

| Where | What runs there |
|---|---|
| Deck | Kokoro-FastAPI on CPU, Ollama on Vulkan, the clip lane, ffmpeg with hardware encode. Systemd user units, sleep disabled on the dock. |
| This Mac | Script via the claude CLI, stills on Metal, assembly, the launcher. |

**How the knobs land.** Your standing rule holds: a new knob goes in `scripts/params.py` only, so the URL and host parameters appear in the profile schema and the launcher forms without separate UI work.

**What I would not build.** A queue or scheduler such as Ray or Celery. A one-person pipeline of four steps does not need a broker, and every one of them would add a daemon that must be alive before anything renders.

**The three risks.** SteamOS updates erase anything outside home, so the Deck's Python lives in a uv venv and its services in user units. The claude CLI must be logged in on the Deck for the clip lane's scoring, or that lane uses the Ollama fallback there. And tailnet names must resolve on both machines, which MagicDNS gives you if it is on.

This is a design, not a change. Say the word and I lay out the edits.

Scopes are the three places Claude Code reads the on/off setting from, and which one wins.

- **User scope** is `~/.claude/settings.json`. It applies to every folder on this machine. Right now it says gamedev, art and video are off, and says nothing about the other four, which means on.
- **Project scope** is `.claude/settings.json` inside a folder, committed to git. It applies to sessions started in that folder and reaches anyone who clones the repo. game-venture's says gamedev, art and video are on. That's why those three are on there and off everywhere else.
- **Local scope** is `.claude/settings.local.json` at the repo root, gitignored. Same reach as project scope but private to you. Nothing uses it yet.

When two disagree, local beats project, and project beats user. A folder with no file of its own just gets the user setting. That's what I called inheriting: 56 of your 58 folders have no settings at all, so they show whatever user scope says.

So the second question, in plain terms: should the graph draw a line from all 56 inheriting folders to the same groups, or draw one line from each to a single "user scope" node that then connects to the groups, with direct folder-to-group lines only for the two folders that have their own file? No. It will not survive updates, and the location can't be moved — Mozilla's own docs say the AutoConfig file location "cannot be changed." On macOS it must live inside `Firefox.app/Contents/Resources`, and a Firefox update replaces that whole bundle. The files go with it.

**What that means in practice:**

- Firefox updates roughly every 4 weeks, so expect it to break about monthly.
- It breaks silently. No error, no warning — the button is just gone one morning.
- Fixing it is re-running the same command. Your extensions and profile are untouched; only the button disappears.

That's the one real cost of this route, and it's inherent — not something I can engineer away.

**Three ways to live with it:**

1. **Notice and re-run.** `firefox-reload-button install`. You'd find out the first time you clicked and nothing happened.
2. **Check on demand.** `firefox-reload-button status` says whether it's still installed. Useful but you have to remember to ask.
3. **Automate it.** A launchd agent watching `/Applications/Firefox.app/Contents/Info.plist` — that file changes on every update — re-running `install` when it does. Reliable, and you'd never think about it again. It's a small plist and one line of config; I haven't built it.

Option 3 is what I'd want if this is going to be a permanent part of your setup. Options 1 and 2 mean the button quietly stops working and you rediscover why each time.

Sources: [Customize Firefox using AutoConfig](https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/customizing-firefox-using-autoconfig) · [Deploy Firefox customizations on macOS](https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/deploying-firefox-customizations-macos)

Read the prep doc (slide 4 is "Six words they grade on") and inspected your actual Dash install. Here is what matters.

## The verdict

Dash is the only lookup tool that is unambiguously fine in a **"no AI, screen share"** round. It is offline documentation — the same thing as the man pages already on the machine. A browser tab is not: on a shared screen, a browser is a thing an interviewer has to trust the contents of. Dash isn't.

Its value is concentrated almost entirely in the **21:00 pair hour**. The 22:00 design hour is talking; you will not look anything up.

## What you already have (verified)

| Docset | Entries | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 14,695 | every symbol on your `cheatsheet.md` — `defaultdict`, `quantize`, `fromisoformat`, `bisect_right`, `heappush`, `token_urlsafe`, `move_to_end` all resolve |
| pytest | 1,096 | `parametrize` (16), `fixture` (101), `raises`, `approx`, `monkeypatch` |
| PostgreSQL | 4,000 | `INSERT`, `CREATE TABLE`, advisory locks, `EXPLAIN`, `date_trunc` |
| NodeJS / TypeScript | 4,788 / 433 | `node:test`, `assert` |

Nothing is missing. Don't spend the afternoon downloading docsets.

## Setup — ten minutes, do it before your next drill

**1. Set the global shortcut. It is currently unset** — I checked the prefs; there is no hotkey stored, so right now Dash is just another ⌘-Tab target, which is worthless mid-flow. Settings → General. `⌥Space` is free on this machine (no Alfred, no Raycast installed). Your keyboard, your call.

**2. Search profiles — the feature that actually matters.** Settings → Docsets → Search Profiles. You have only the two stock ones. Create:

| Profile | Docsets | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Python | Python + pytest | app-activation on VS Code, plus keyword `py:` |
| SQL | PostgreSQL | keyword `sql:` |
| TS | Node.js + TypeScript | keyword `ts:` |

App activation is the point: when VS Code is frontmost, Dash searches Python and pytest only. No Node results polluting a Python lookup at minute 40 when your attention is thin.

**3. VS Code extension** — `deerawan.vscode-dash`, 1.3M installs. Bindings from its manifest:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| `⌃H` | search the selection / word under cursor in the language's docset |
| `⌃⌥H` | search it across all docsets |

Cursor on `parametrize` → `⌃H` → signature. No window switching, which is what makes it invisible on a screen share.

**4. Keywords are already assigned** (from your screenshot): `python:`, `pytest:`, `psql:`, `nodejs:`, `typescript:`.

## The lookups that will actually happen tonight

| Moment | Type this |
|---|---|
| `field(default_factory=...)` | `python:dataclasses`, then ⌘F "field" |
| Decimal rounding constant | `python:quantize` |
| `@parametrize` argument order | `pytest:parametrize` |
| `raises(..., match=)` | `pytest:raises` |
| tier lookup | `python:bisect_right` |
| fake clock / monotonic | `python:monotonic` |
| `ON CONFLICT` syntax | `psql:INSERT`, then ⌘F "ON CONFLICT" |
| node test runner | `nodejs:test` |

That last row is a real gotcha: the PostgreSQL docset indexes **commands, not clauses**. `tstzrange` returns zero hits; `INSERT` returns seven. Search the command, then find within the page. ⌥↓/⌥↑ walks the table of contents.

## Rules of engagement on the screen share

- **Say it once, at the start**: "I keep the docs offline in Dash — I'll look up signatures rather than guess." It reframes every lookup as method instead of floundering, and it costs one sentence.
- **Budget two lookups per twenty minutes.** Your prep doc says silence is the main failure mode of a pair round. A person reading docs is a person not narrating. Dash's job is to shorten the silence, not to create it.
- **Look up signatures, never approaches.** If you're browsing to work out *how* to do something, you're lost — say that out loud instead. That's a better minute than a silent one.
- **Keep talking while it's open.** "Checking the argument order on parametrize" is a full sentence and it keeps the room with you.

## Snippets — my recommendation is: one, or none

Snippets are disabled in your current profile (`snippetsAreEnabledForCurrentProfile = 0`). They expand in *any* app, so a stray abbreviation can dump code into the shared editor at a bad moment, and a finished block appearing in a single keystroke reads poorly on a screen share whatever the stated rules are.

If you enable anything, enable exactly one: the pytest file header — imports plus a first failing test — so minute 0–2 is spent writing the test, not the imports. Give it a symbol-prefixed abbreviation (Kapeli's own advice) like `;pyt`, never a bare word. Placeholders are `__name__`, with `@cursor` for the landing point.

## Between now and 21:00

You have four hours and the drill window in your doc has passed. Do your remaining drills **with the real constraint**: Dash and `cheatsheet.md` open, browser closed, no AI. The point isn't learning Dash's UI — it's that at minute 40, under pressure, your hand goes to `⌥Space` instead of to a browser. That reflex is the whole deliverable.

The trial is fully functional for 30 days; it will not nag you tonight.

drive-survey mft /Volumes/Elements <workdir> mft.bin
```

It finds the device from the mount point and asks for your `sudo` password once. With `--unmount` it frees the drive for the copy and mounts it again afterwards, even if the copy fails or you press Ctrl-C. At the end it checks the copy's size against what `$MFT` declares.

Everything except the real `sudo` copy is tested: the size check, device lookup, progress copy, and the remount in every failure case. The copy itself runs the same command that worked for you earlier. The scratch script it replaces will be deleted with the session.

The survey is complete. The report and its data are here:

~/dev/notebook/2026-09-15-elements-drive-survey/report.html

**What gauntlet-loop is**

One markdown file. No code. It writes a prompt for you. You give a goal, it suggests two or three reference works to beat, you pick one, and it hands you a short prompt to paste into a fresh session. The idea comes from Matt Shumer's Claude of Duty project.

**The loop that prompt sets up**

1. Pick a bar. A real, named thing the agent can fetch: a specific game's footage, a specific live page, a specific repo and its benchmark. Vague bars are refused.
2. Split the goal into small pieces that can each be judged on their own.
3. For each piece, one agent builds and a second agent with no shared context judges. The judge looks at the real output next to the reference, labels hidden, and picks the better one. It also names the biggest remaining gap. No scores, only a pick.
4. Repeat until the judge picks ours. There is no round limit. It stops when it wins or when you stop it.
5. The prompt says nothing about stack, architecture, or file layout. The agent decides those.

**What the source project says about its own result**

Claude of Duty's README says plainly that it did not reach Call of Duty quality. Eleven judges compared it blind against the real game over four rounds. Every judge, every round, picked the real game. Scores went from 3.6 to 5.1 out of 10. So the loop never hit its exit condition. The author stopped it.

The good results people posted come from a loop that never won. The game looks good because it is a lot of procedural rendering code, worked on for a long time.

The README credits the tooling, not the prompt, for the quality: repeatable screenshots that come out identical every run, a pixel-diff check, a profiler that reports worst frames and explains each stall, and an architecture file the agents worked against. Their earlier performance numbers were wrong until the tooling was fixed. Same lesson as the Astra post.

**Astra loop versus gauntlet loop**

- Astra: you play and say what is wrong. The agent measures and fixes.
- Gauntlet: a second agent judges instead of you, against a real reference. This is the useful part. It runs without you, and blind comparison is a much better judge than an agent grading itself.
- The gauntlet's problem is the bar. Against a AAA game it cannot win, so "loop until it wins" becomes "loop until you run out of money." Against a bar you can actually beat, such as one screen from a specific indie game, the loop ends on quality.
- Neither is an advantage anyone else has. The gauntlet is a paragraph. Subagents and looping are available right here.

**What to use**

Builder plus fresh-context judge, on small pieces, against a beatable named reference. Add the Astra-style tooling so the judge compares captures, not impressions. The game-ui-refs skill in this repo already fetches named references for UI screens, which is the bar half of this.

That list spans four operating systems, which narrows the field fast. Two identifications first: there is no Surface Book 7. A 2020 model is a Surface Book 3, which shipped with an i7-1065G7 and an optional GTX 1650 or 1660 Ti in the keyboard base. Whether yours has that base decides the plan, so I have assumed it does. I also assumed the Air is Apple Silicon.

**What each device contributes**

| Device | Useful for | OS path | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Surface Book 3 | LLM head node | Linux via WSL2 with mirrored networking, or dual-boot with the linux-surface kernel | The only CUDA GPU in the set. Fastest decode. Should hold the most layers. |
| Steam Deck | LLM worker, k3s node | SteamOS as-is. Deck is Arch, llama.cpp builds with Vulkan on the RDNA2 iGPU | 16 GB shared memory, real GPU. Second-best node. |
| MacBook Air | LLM worker | macOS as-is, Metal backend | Unified memory, fast per watt. Third node. |
| Pixel 3a | k3s node only | postmarketOS. Pixel 3a (sargo) is a well-supported device and the June 2026 writeup used exactly this phone | 4 GB RAM, Snapdragon 670. Too weak to help inference over Wi-Fi. |
| Redmi Pad 2 | Marginal | Termux only. Xiaomi bootloader unlock is throttled and MediaTek has no postmarketOS port | Can run a prima.cpp or cake worker, but a scheduler will drop it. |

**Pooled inference: prima.cpp**

It is the only project built for this exact shape: mixed CPU and GPU, insufficient RAM, Wi-Fi, disk offload, and automatic removal of devices that slow the ring down. The head runs on the Surface under WSL2. Workers run on the Deck, the Air, and optionally the two Android devices via Termux. With the Surface, Deck and Air pooled you have roughly 40 GB across the three, which puts a 32B Q4 model comfortably in memory and a 70B Q4 within reach using its prefetching disk offload. Its limitation is model coverage: Llama, Qwen and DeepSeek families only.

If you need arbitrary GGUF models, the fallback is the stock llama.cpp RPC backend. It runs natively on all four OSes including Termux, but you set the layer split by hand and every node must be the same build.

exo is out because it has no Windows or Android support and runs CPU-only on Linux. cake covers every OS you own but has less activity and no heterogeneity-aware scheduling.

**General compute: k3s**

Steam Deck as control plane, Pixel 3a as an agent on postmarketOS. Expect the nftables and kernel-module rabbit holes every writeup hit, though sargo has a mature port so the kernel side should be cleaner than the OnePlus stories. The Redmi Pad joins only through DroidNode, which is a proof of concept with no volumes or restart policies. The Air stays out of k3s; it earns more as an inference node than as a Linux VM host.

**Two facts I need from you** to finalize: does the Surface Book 3 have the dGPU base, and which chip and RAM is in the Air? Without the dGPU, the Deck becomes the head node and the Surface drops to a CPU worker.

**What was built, in asset-pipeline**

- **Address knobs.** `KOKORO_URL` and `OLLAMA_URL` in the local config, read by both the pipeline and pipectl, defaulting to this machine. `KOKORO_BIND` lets the Kokoro launcher listen beyond localhost on the aiding host.

- **The loop.** `pipectl work` scans every piece and the request queue, claims what it may, runs the ordinary `pipectl video <step>` command, waits for the job, and releases. column2:
Audit done. Here's what I found and changed.

**Exactly one line in the extension can reach the network:** `walker.js:66`. Everything else either wraps requests the page was already making, or writes `data:` URLs to disk — the export steps, including the 150-file document export, make **zero** server requests.

**Three defects found, all fixed:**

1. **Frame fan-out.** Content scripts run with `all_frames: true`, and a tab-wide `chrome.tabs.sendMessage` reaches every frame. Each frame would have started its own walker — an N-way parallel run. Now: walker refuses to install outside the top frame, *and* the worker dispatches with `{frameId: 0}`. Two independent guards.
2. **Repeated Sorgula multiplied the plan.** Each press leaves another list response in the store, and I was concatenating rows across all of them. Three presses over overlapping cases meant planning the same case three times. Now deduped by `(endpoint, id)` before the cap.
3. **Nested objects counted as cases.** The row collector recursed into each row, so `dosyadakiBilirkisiler` and `altBilirkisiYetkiList` entries — which also carry a `dosyaId` — were harvested as additional cases. Recursion now stops at the first array of objects.

**The limits now in the code**, each with a test:

| | |
|---|---|
| Concurrency | 1, sequential `await` — never parallel |
| Spacing | 1.0s / 1.2s / 2.5s by step, with an 800 ms floor the caller cannot undercut |
| Cap per run | 1 / 400 / 150. Worst case: step 2 is 8 minutes, step 3 is ~6 minutes and under 100 MB |
| Retries | none — a failure is counted and skipped, never re-sent |
| 429 or 503 | run halts immediately |
| Consecutive failures | 3 and it halts |
| Concurrent runs | refused twice over: worker-side state, and the page-side `running` flag |
| Already captured | never planned again |
| Timers | none. No `chrome.alarms`, no auto-start, nothing runs unless a button is pressed twice |

At 1.2s spacing the walker is **slower than a person clicking** — opening one case by hand fires four or five requests inside a second.

**Residual risks I can't close from here:**

- **It has never touched the real server.** If UYAP requires a single-use token per request, the replays will be rejected — which the 3-consecutive-failure guard turns into an automatic stop after three requests, not a hammering. That is the designed failure mode, but it is untested against the live portal.
- **If UYAP treats any scripted access as abuse regardless of rate**, no amount of throttling helps. That judgment is yours; the passive capture alone never replays anything.
- **Service-worker sleep** mid-walk resets the progress display. The page-side lock still holds, so no second walk can start — the readout just goes stale until a refresh.

33/33 tests pass. `uyap-kayit-1.2.0.zip` is rebuilt. My recommendation for the first live run: use step 1 alone, which is a single request, and confirm it comes back with real data before letting step 2 near a list of 400.

It's a **Codex skill** built on a numbered library of 261 hand-drawn styles. You pick a number from the contact sheets and ask the agent for something like `041号风格，主题：<subject>` ("style 041, theme: …"). You get back a Chinese and an English prompt to paste into any image model. If the agent can generate images and you ask it to, the skill also decides whether to attach that style's reference image.

**What it produces.** I ran the bundled script:

```
Selected style: #041 · Bendy Absurd Storybook
Style name: #041 · Bendy Absurd Storybook. Theme: the first cup of milk tea in autumn. Reference author/style name: Dr. Seuss. aspect ratio: 3:4.
```

The prompt is deliberately short: style name, your subject, and the real illustrator the style is based on. The real value is `references/styles.json`, which maps each number to an illustrator, a style name and Chinese notes on the look. There is also one reference image per style under `images/individual/`.

**How to use it**

| Where | Setup | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Codex (what it was built for) | Put `handdraw-style-prompter/` in `~/.agents/skills/` or a repo's `.agents/skills/`, then call it with `$handdraw-style-prompter` | `SKILL.md` hardcodes Windows paths (`E:\handraw-style\…`), so they have to point at your clone instead. Opening the gallery automatically relies on a tool that only exists in the Codex app. |
| Claude Code | Put the same folder in `~/.claude/skills/` | Only the prompt-writing part works, since Claude Code has no image-generation tool. The Codex gallery call and the `E:\` fallback link won't do anything. |
| No agent | Pick a number from the GitHub README, run `python3 scripts/prompt_style.py --style 041 --theme "…"`, or give `images/individual/001-200/041.png` to any image model that accepts a style reference image | The README shows every contact sheet, so it works as the gallery |

For your setup, `/trial-skill install yang0/handraw-style handdraw-style-prompter` is enough for Claude Code. It only fetches that subfolder, so the 99 MB `images/` folder stays behind. Writing prompts doesn't need the images, and the README covers browsing.

**What's broken (I tested a clone)**
- **Missing module:** `resolve_reference.py`, the script that decides whether to attach an image, crashes with `ModuleNotFoundError: style_asset_paths` because that module was never committed. `validate_library.py` and `split_contact_sheets.py` import it too, so they fail the same way.
- **One model only:** the table of what each image model can do covers only `gpt-image-2`. Any other model is treated as unknown, so the reference image always gets attached.
- **Outdated numbers:** `agents/openai.yaml` and `MANIFEST.md` still say 001–217.
- **Rough script output:** `prompt_style.py` just fills in a template, and it dropped my English theme straight into the Chinese prompt. The skill tells the agent to write natural prompts instead of copying the script's output.

Because you have keyboard navigation turned on in macOS, and the app never says which control should have focus when its window opens.

- `AppleKeyboardUIMode` is `2` on this Mac, meaning System Settings → Keyboard → **Keyboard navigation** is on. With it on, buttons can take keyboard focus. With it off, they can't, and this ring wouldn't appear.
- `mac/PadBridge.swift` never sets `initialFirstResponder` and never calls `makeFirstResponder`. It only calls `window.makeKeyAndOrderFront(nil)` at line 1351. When a window becomes key without a focus target, AppKit builds the Tab order itself and focuses the first view that accepts focus. Here that's **Send clipboard**, the first button in the view tree.

So it's more than looks: pressing Space right after launch would press that button and send your clipboard to the pad.

To fix it, the app would call `window.makeFirstResponder(nil)` after `makeKeyAndOrderFront`, so the window itself holds focus and no control does. Tab would still move into the buttons. ⌘V would still work, since it goes through the menu.

Three things, and only one of them is a real bar.

**1. An organization — but that's lower than it sounds.** Approval is scoped to an Organization ID, not a user. Every Claude account has one (Settings → Account or Settings → Organization). It does not have to be a company plan; it does mean approval doesn't follow you into a different workspace.

**2. Identity-verified.** Mandatory, via Persona:

| Applying as | Required |
|---|---|
| Individual | Original government photo ID (passport, driver's licence, national ID) + possibly a live selfie |
| Organization | Legal name, address, **business registration number**, plus a representative's photo ID |

Photocopies, screenshots and digital IDs are rejected — physical document only.

**3. Not on Zero Data Retention.** That's the only hard exclusion the help centre names. ZDR accounts are ineligible; sales-managed ZDR goes through your rep instead.

**What you have to demonstrate:** a legitimate *defensive* purpose. Named-acceptable: authorized pentesting, vulnerability research, exploitability analysis, red teaming, threat intelligence, CTF. Anthropic says it weighs who's applying, what you build, and how you intend to use the access.

- **Geography.** One search summary asserted CVP is currently limited to a set of US organizations. I could not find that sentence on any Anthropic page — the help centre lists ZDR as the sole exclusion, and the US-organizations framing appears to belong to Project Glasswing (a separate, much narrower Mythos access program). Treat it as unconfirmed; the form will tell you.

- [Real-time cyber safeguards on Claude Opus and Sonnet](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-real-time-cyber-safeguards-on-claude-opus-and-sonnet)

You're right — drop the extension. It only does anything inside VS Code. Whatever you're typing in, the move is the same: ⌘Tab to Dash, ⌘L, type, ⌘Tab back.

## The one habit that makes lookups work

**Type `module.symbol`, not just `symbol`.** The Python docset includes the C API, so bare words collide badly:

| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| `python:field` | `PyStructSequence_Desc.fields`, `ctypes.CField.bit_offset`, namedtuple `_fields`… |
| `python:dataclasses.field` | `dataclasses.field` — the one you wanted |
| `python:monotonic` | `PyTime_MonotonicRaw`, `PyTime_Monotonic`, `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW_APPROX`… |
| `python:time.monotonic` | `time.monotonic` |

## Worked examples from tonight's problems

**Minute 6 — you're writing the `Event` dataclass and need a list default.**

```
python:dataclasses.field
```

Result list shows `dataclasses.field` (Function). The page has the `default_factory` signature. If you also want to see what else is in the module, search `python:dataclasses.` with the trailing dot — you'll get `dataclass`, `field`, `fields`, `asdict`, `astuple`, `KW_ONLY`, `MISSING`, `__post_init__`.

**Minute 12 — first table of test cases.**

```
pytest:parametrize
```

Two kinds of result come back, and the difference matters:

- `@pytest.mark.parametrize: parametrizing test functions` — a **Section** from the how-to guide. Worked examples. This is what you want.
- `pytest.Metafunc.parametrize` — the **Method**. Internals. Not what you want.

Rule of thumb: Guide/Section entries answer *how do I write this*, Function/Method entries answer *what are the arguments*. For decorators you almost always want the guide, because `pytest.mark.parametrize` isn't in the API reference at all — I checked. `mark.skip`, `skipif`, `xfail`, `usefixtures` are there; `parametrize` only exists in the guide page.

**Minute 20 — money rounding.**

```
python:Decimal.quantize
```

Gives `decimal.Decimal.quantize`. On that page, ⌘F "ROUND" to see the rounding modes in context. Or go straight at the constant: `python:decimal.ROUND_HALF_UP` — the whole family (`ROUND_CEILING`, `ROUND_FLOOR`, `ROUND_HALF_EVEN`, `ROUND_05UP`) is indexed individually.

**Minute 25 — token bucket, fake clock.**

```
python:time.monotonic
```

**Minute 30 — interviewer says "now handle duplicate event ids".**

You look up nothing. You say "I'll key by event id in a dict, so a retry is a no-op" and type it. This is the moment where opening Dash costs you the round — it's a design answer, not an API question. Knowing when *not* to search is most of the skill.

**Minute 35 — tiered pricing.**

```
python:bisect.bisect_right
```

The bisect page carries the worked grade-lookup example, which is exactly the tier-boundary pattern.

**Minute 40 — API keys.**

```
python:secrets.token_urlsafe
python:hashlib.sha256
```

**If you go the TypeScript route instead:**

```
nodejs:test

## Design round, if you sketch SQL

```

```

then ⌘F "ON CONFLICT". The clause isn't indexed on its own — I checked, `tstzrange` returns zero hits — because the PostgreSQL docset indexes one page per **command**. Search the command, find inside the page.

Advisory locks are the exception, they're indexed as functions:

```
psql:advisory
```

returns `Advisory Lock Functions`, `pg_advisory_lock`, `pg_advisory_xact_lock`.

## When a search comes back wrong

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| C API junk fills the list | qualify it: `python:time.monotonic`, not `python:monotonic` |
| SQL clause returns nothing | search the command, then ⌘F |
| Decorator isn't in the API list | take the Guide/Section result instead |

column1: # next: claude, if I loaded any video compression app for regular consumers, what default compression takes place?

column2:
Four levers. Here's what each is actually worth, measured on your file rather than guessed:

| Lever | Measured impact | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Codec** H.264 → HEVC | 9.5 GB → 5.6 GB, same quality | The big win. Free on your TV. |
| **Bitrate / quality** | CRF 26 → 28: 5.6 → 4.3 GB | Real, and where you tune. |
| **Encoder effort** hardware → x265 | ~10% smaller, **4x the time** | Poor trade here. |
| **Framerate** 50 → 25 fps | **8%** | Dead lever. Costs smoothness for nothing. |
| **Resolution** 1080p → 720p | Not measured | Large, but visible on a TV. Would sample before trusting it. |

The reason compression works so well here: your camcorder wrote 10.4 Mbps with **no B-frames at all**. It was buying realtime encoding with bitrate. Any modern encoder reclaims most of that before quality even enters the conversation.

**The options, measured:**

| | Encoder | Size | Time | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | HW HEVC @ 3800k | **~5.1 GB** | 35-60 min | Fits internal, watchable tonight |
| **B** | HW HEVC @ 3000k | ~4.1 GB * | 35-60 min | If free space is tighter than you think |
| **C** | HW HEVC @ 6000k | ~7.9 GB * | 35-60 min | USB only. Best picture per minute spent. |
| **D** | x265 CRF 26 | 5.6 GB | ~3 h | Better picture than A at similar size |
| **E** | x265 CRF 28 | 4.3 GB | ~3 h | Better picture than B at similar size |
| **F** | x264 CRF 23 | 9.5 GB | ~4 h | Max compatibility — unnecessary, your TV does HEVC |

\* B and C are scaled from A's measured 3.96 Mbps, not separately sampled. A, D, E and F are real sampled numbers.

**My recommendation is A.** Not because it's the best compression — D is — but because three hours of x265 buys about 10% that nobody sees from a sofa, and you want to watch this with family tonight.

If USB is possible, **C instead**: same encode time, noticeably better picture, and the 12 GB ceiling stops mattering.

It came back. Its answer, faithfully:

**"Atlas has no server-side application at all."** The deploy is `nginx:alpine` serving a static directory. All state is one blob, `data.json`, produced by the local scanner, pulled and pushed over scp. The viewer is a pure reader.

**It splits the state in two**, and says these should not share a mechanism:

- **Observed inventory** — regenerated wholesale every scan. Already solved; a database adds nothing to a blob that gets rewritten anyway.
- **Page state** — pins, and whatever page-side preferences follow. Tiny, ordered-list-shaped, single-household, low-write. This is what has no home.

**Its recommendation:** replace `nginx:alpine` with a ~60-line server in the same container slot — serves the static directory exactly as nginx does, plus `GET /api/pins` and `PUT /api/pins` writing a `pins.json` beside `data.json`, atomic write via rename. Authelia's `forward_auth` already gates every request, so the endpoint needs no auth code of its own. Then move pin *application* out of the scanner into the viewer: `App.tsx` fetches both files and orders the page at render time.

**What it would not do:** no SQLite or Postgres ("architecture cosplay" for one ordered list of strings); no localStorage, since pins belong to the atlas rather than one browser; no git-backed state, because repo file plus CLI is exactly what you called impractical twice; and no general read-write API over the inventory — keeping `pins.json` a separate file means the scp push and the browser's PUT can never clobber each other.

Its one-line answer to your question: atlas was built write-once-from-the-laptop, and that assumption expired the moment the page became interactive.

Two things worth flagging where this lands against what I had:

It corrected me on the container. I was about to add a **second** service beside nginx with a Caddy path route; replacing nginx outright is simpler — one container, no route change, the static serving is a dozen lines of stdlib.

And it caught a real inconsistency in what I built: `pins.py`'s own docstring says a pin changes where something sits on the page, but `atlas pin` routes every pin through a scan-and-push. The docstring describes the design; the implementation contradicts it. Moving pin application into the viewer is what makes the docstring true.

Your call on whether to build it.

column1: # next: say it simpler and shorter

column2:
Four moving parts, one file connecting them.

## The problem

Two of the three machines involved sleep. Your Mac is shut half the time; node01 is always on. A backup that only exists on node01 dies with node01, and a copy pulled to your Mac is only as good as the pulling still happening. Nothing could tell you it had stopped.

## The three timers

**node01, 18:00 UTC daily** — `vikunja-backup.timer` takes a hot copy of `vikunja.db` through SQLite's backup API, runs `integrity_check` on it, and only then rotates out anything older than 14 days. Next run Fri 18:00.

**Your Mac, every 6 hours and at login** — `com.mrtysn.vikunja-backup-pull` rsyncs the dated files down to `~/Backups/node01/vikunja/`, without `--delete`, so this Mac accumulates everything while the box rotates at 14. It then opens the newest file and counts rows. Last exit 0.

**node01, every 15 minutes** — `node01-health.timer`, which already existed.

## The stamp — the part that makes it self-watching

After a successful pull, your Mac writes one line back onto the box:

```
1788465719 mrtysn-mbp-m2max      ← 14 minutes ago
```

`/var/backups/vikunja/.last-pulled` — epoch seconds plus which machine did it.

`node01-health` now reads that file as one more check alongside disk and containers. If it's older than 72 hours, the pull has stopped and you get a Telegram message. Right now it's 14 minutes old, so you get nothing — silence means healthy, as with every other check.

**Why this direction and not the obvious one.** The natural instinct is to have the box check on the Mac. It can't: nothing on node01 can reach a laptop, and the laptop is unreachable precisely when it's broken or asleep — the two states you most need to tell apart. So the intermittent machine reports in, and the always-on machine judges the report. The box never needs to reach anything.

## What you'd actually see

| What breaks | What happens |
|---|---|
| Backup script fails on the box | Telegram, that night — the script alerts on its own failure |
| launchd agent dies, or you stop using this Mac | Telegram after 72h: *"Vikunja backups not pulled off-box for 76h (last from mrtysn-mbp-m2max)"* |
| Mac shut for a weekend | Nothing. 72h is chosen to sit above a long weekend |
| A pulled file is corrupt | The pull exits 1 and refuses to stamp, so the check-in goes stale and you're told within 72h |
| node01 dies entirely | No message — a dead box can't send one. That's what the daily heartbeat is for: its absence is the signal |

## The knobs

`VIKUNJA_PULL_MAX_AGE_H` in `/opt/monitoring/.env` moves the 72h. `VIKUNJA_BACKUP_KEEP` moves the 14 days on the box. Neither affects this Mac's archive, which keeps everything.

## What you asked for

A Firefox equivalent of the Chrome extension that reloads all unpacked extensions from one pinned toolbar icon.

## What was established

**It cannot be a Firefox extension.** `management.setEnabled()` returns an error for anything but themes. That's the whole reason no such add-on exists.

Routes tried and dropped, each for a concrete reason:

| Route | Why not |
|---|---|
| Debug port (RDP) | Works — I reloaded two extensions with it — but Firefox only opens the port on a cold start with a flag. Workflow-breaking. |
| `web-ext run` | Auto-reloads on save, but launches its own instance, one extension at a time. |
| Sign / Developer Edition | Fixes restarts, but a permanent extension loses the Reload button entirely. |
| **AutoConfig** | Privileged startup JS inside `Firefox.app`. Real toolbar button, no port, no flag, no restart, no profile change. |

## What got built

```
~/dev/dev-env/bin/firefox-reload-button
~/dev/dev-env/firefox/mozilla.cfg
~/dev/dev-env/firefox/autoconfig.js
```

A toolbar button plus `Cmd+Alt+E`, both calling `addon.reload()` on every temporarily-installed extension — the same call `about:debugging`'s Reload button makes. The installer does `install` / `uninstall` / `status`, takes a bundle path, and refuses to overwrite an AutoConfig it didn't write.

Verified headlessly against a duplicate of your Firefox 154: widget registers in the navbar, icon binds, key element installs, both test extensions reload, install/uninstall round-trips clean, no errors.

## Outstanding

1. **Install it** — I'm blocked from writing to `/Applications/Firefox.app`:
   `! ~/dev/dev-env/bin/firefox-reload-button install`
   then restart Firefox.
2. **Commit the three files** — currently uncommitted in `dev-env`.
3. **Symlink into `~/bin`** if you want it as a bare command.
4. **Two things untested**: how the button looks, and the keystroke actually firing. Both need a GUI I didn't want stealing your screen.

## Where I wasted your time

I spent a long stretch on the debug-port route before establishing it needed a cold start, then pushed a hot/cold read of your two repos that I'd inferred from file timestamps — which you corrected. The AutoConfig option was available from the start and I reached it late.

Fair question, and thinking it through changes my answer.

A Google Cloud project is a container: the APIs you enabled, the OAuth clients you created, the consent screen, and the daily API quota. It costs nothing, and clients inside it are independent of each other; revoking one never touches another. I suggested reuse because it meant one consent screen to maintain.

Two things argue the other way, and they outweigh that:

- **Quota is per project.** YouTube gives each project 10,000 units a day, and one upload costs 1,600, so a project uploads about six shorts a day before it must apply for more. Twenty channels will need that increase, and Google grants it per project with a review of what the project does. That review should be about the channels, not entangled with a wedding app's sign-in.
- **Blast radius.** If Google ever restricts the project, for a quota dispute, a policy flag on the upload scope, or a failed verification, everything in it stops: event-faces' Google sign-in would go down with the shorts. Separate projects fail separately.

**Python API** — `tab.async_set_title()`, the programmatic form of right-click → Edit Tab Title. That one sets `titleOverride`, which genuinely beats OSC titles. column2:
Yes — three of them, and one is genuinely actionable for you now.

The way to think about it: sweating is a chain, and you can break it at any link.

| Where | Method |
|---|---|
| The nerve chain in the chest | ETS surgery |
| The nerve ending, where it releases acetylcholine | Botox |
| The receptor on the gland | anticholinergic pills; topical gels |
| **Inside the duct** | **aluminium chloride (chemical) · iontophoresis (electrical)** |
| Destroy the gland outright | miraDry, Brella patch — underarms only |

Iontophoresis and the cream are neighbours. They do roughly the same thing at the same place.

## The closest non-electrical version — and it's better than what I told you

Aluminium chloride works by hydrolysing on the skin into a gel plug inside the duct, and it releases HCl while doing it. So it plugs *and* acidifies — the same two things the anode does. The reason it fails on palms isn't the mechanism, it's that it can't get through thick palm skin.

Three things fix the penetration, and they stack:

1. **30% instead of 20%.** The literature says palms specifically need up to 30%.
2. **A salicylic acid base.** [Benohanian, 1998, 238 patients](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1365-4362.1998.00543.x): people who had *failed* aluminium chloride in plain alcohol, or couldn't tolerate it, improved when it was put in a salicylic acid gel instead. Salicylic acid thins the dead outer layer, so the aluminium gets down the duct.
3. **Occlusion.** Cotton or vinyl gloves over your hands overnight, 6–8 hours.

Now look at the Turkish majistral formula again:

> Aluminium chloride **30 g** · **salicylic acid 2.5 g** · propylene glycol 9 g · ethanol to 100 g

That's items 1 and 2 already, in a formula your dermatologist can write. Add gloves and you have the maximal topical protocol — the closest thing to iontophoresis that involves no machine, no import, and no build.

The catch is the same as always: occlusion amplifies the effect and amplifies the irritation, sometimes severely. Start without the gloves, add them if you tolerate it.

## If you do end up with a machine, don't use plain water

This changes the machine's value considerably. [Dolianitis 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15527429/?dopt=Abstract), 20 patients, left-versus-right on the same person:

| What's in the water | Median days of dry hands |
|---|---|
| Tap water | **3** |
| Glycopyrrolate, one side | **5** |
| Glycopyrrolate, both sides | **11** |

All differences statistically significant. Nearly four times the duration.

Which makes sense — iontophoresis was invented as a *drug delivery* method. Using it to drive an actual anticholinergic into the skin is what the technique is for; tap water is the stripped-down version. It also means the maintenance schedule everyone on ekşi complains about (a session every 8–14 days) gets considerably easier.

One caveat: bilateral beating unilateral means some of it is working systemically, so the dry-mouth side effect isn't fully avoided.

## What's new since 2024, and why it doesn't help you

- **Sofdra** (sofpironium bromide 12.45% gel), FDA-approved June 2024 — over 60% of patients got a ≥50% cut in sweating
- **Brella / TAT patch**, approved 2023
- Both were called potential first-line options at the 2025 AAD meeting

**Both are approved for underarms only.** Nothing new has landed for palms. Don't chase them.

Mechanistic footnote you'll appreciate: the Brella patch works by "targeted alkali thermolysis" — an alkali reaction on the skin. That's the *cathode* chemistry from our earlier conversation, commercialised. Someone took the half of iontophoresis you'd normally treat as a nuisance and built a product out of it.

column2: I sent `dev-c6` a short question asking how to run their disk-reading tool on node01, and told them to ignore my earlier one. I'll use the tool as soon as they reply.

It won't change page load times in any way a guest would notice. What limits page loads today is event-faces' 2 web workers and the internet path, not the disk. Here's the full reasoning, request by request, using the real file sizes and code on node01.

**How pages are served**

| App | How images are served | Files a page reads |
|---|---|---|
| eclendim | Threaded Python server, so image requests run in parallel; thumbnails lazy-load | thumbnails 35 KB, lightbox images 436 KB, originals only for zip downloads (14.6 MB each) |
| event-faces | Every image goes through Django on **2 synchronous gunicorn workers**, so at most two image requests are handled at once, across all visitors | grid images ~25 KB, web images ~290 KB, originals for zips |

**Each kind of request**

1. **Thumbnails and lightbox images**
   - The images pages actually show come to about 1.3 GB in total (eclendim 671 MB, event-faces 482 MB, the new wedding ~150 MB).
   - node01 has ~2 GB of memory the system uses to cache recently read files, so most of that set sits in RAM after its first view. Cached reads never touch storage, whether local disk or volume.
   - An uncached thumbnail read from local disk measured ~2 ms. Network storage typically adds roughly 1–4 ms per small read. Hetzner doesn't publish a figure, so that range is an industry norm, not a Hetzner number.
   - The page itself takes 165–250 ms to reach Turkey, so a few extra milliseconds disappear.
2. **Lightbox image (436 KB)**
   - The disk reads it in under 5 ms at any plausible volume speed.
   - Sending it to a guest at ~5 MB/s takes ~90 ms. The network dominates.
3. **Zip download (e.g. one person's 50 originals, ~730 MB)**
   - At a ~5 MB/s home connection that's about 2.5 minutes.
   - Any volume reads it in seconds.
   - Only a guest on gigabit fiber could be limited by the volume, and that assumes a speed cap Hetzner doesn't document.
4. **Face processing**
   - Reading a 14.6 MB original costs ~0.15 s at a modest 100 MB/s, against 1.5–3 s of CPU per photo on node01.
   - At most ~10% slower, once, for 459 photos: about a minute.

**The real bottleneck, whatever the storage**

event-faces sends every image and every zip through those 2 workers, and a zip download holds a worker for its whole duration.
- **One zip in progress:** the rest of the site runs on a single worker.
- **Two zips in progress:** every other visitor's images wait until one finishes.

On delivery day, when many guests open their pages and start downloads at once, that will slow pages far more than any disk would. A volume changes nothing here, in either direction.

**What would actually make pages faster**

The volume leaves speed as it is today. **CX33 (+€3.60/month)** is the option that would improve it: double the RAM means more images cached in memory, and there's room to run more web workers.

The sleep one is the only soft answer and it's a ten-second check tomorrow morning.

## Two things in that screenshot I didn't know

**"el ve ayaklar soguk soguk" — feet are involved too, and both run cold.**

Feet changes the build slightly. The single-limb wrist-cathode trick from the Cureus paper handles one hand at a time. Pehlivan's design put the anode on the hands and cathode on the feet, treating all four at once in 20 minutes — which is the more efficient arrangement if you have both, and it's why his device had four electrodes.

Cold-and-wet is also a coherent pairing rather than a separate problem: the sympathetic drive that opens the sweat glands also constricts the peripheral vessels. One of the ekşi users describes exactly this — *"kışın bu durum buz gibi el ayak olarak yansıyor."* Worth mentioning at the appointment.

(One truncated line reads *"sakinim ancak ellerim titri..."* — if that's "titriyor," tremor plus sweating is the pair that points at thyroid. Yours was normal in March, so it's likely nothing, but you can read the full message.)

## Weed + tobacco

**Nicotine is the direct one.** Eccrine sweat glands are sympathetic but *cholinergic* — acetylcholine at the gland. Nicotine acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It's not a vague "stimulants make you sweat" association; it's agonism near the exact pathway that drives your palms. Of everything on your list, this is the one with a mechanism pointed straight at the symptom.

**Cannabis is less direct but not nothing.** Acute THC drives sympathetic activation, and separately, sweating is a listed feature of cannabis withdrawal — so for a daily user, the gap between doses is its own window.

Neither causes primary hyperhidrosis, and stopping either wouldn't fix it. But they sit on top of it, and nicotine noticeably so. Your call what to do with that — it's just worth knowing which lever is which before you spend 40.000 lira on a machine.

column2:
Yes. Found one, and it's clean.

Both pieces verified just now on your Firefox 154:

- `runtime.reload()` re-reads the extension from disk
- The `commands` API registers a real keyboard shortcut on a temporarily-loaded extension — `reload-self=Alt+Shift+R`

## The solution

Add about six lines to each extension. In `manifest.json`:

```json
"commands": {
  "reload-self": {
    "suggested_key": { "default": "Alt+Shift+1" },
    "description": "Reload this extension from disk"
  }
}
```

In the background script:

```js
browser.commands.onCommand.addListener((name) => {
  if (name === "reload-self") { browser.runtime.reload(); }
});
```

Press the key. The extension reloads from disk. That's it.

## Why this is the clean one

| | AutoConfig button | This |
|---|---|---|
| Modifies Firefox.app | Yes | **No** |
| Breaks on Firefox update | Monthly, silently | **Never** |
| Privileged/unsupported code | Yes | **No — documented API** |
| Where it lives | Inside the browser | **In your repos, with your code** |
| Breaks code signature | Yes | **No** |

It's also self-documenting: the shortcut shows up in `about:addons` → Manage Extension Shortcuts, where you can change it without touching code.

`firefox-lens` gets `Alt+Shift+1`, `link-keeper` gets `Alt+Shift+2`. One key each rather than one key for both — which is usually what you want anyway, since you've just edited one of them.

If you genuinely want a single key that reloads both, that's doable via cross-extension messaging (`onMessageExternal`), but I haven't tested it and it adds coordination between two repos for very little.

## About the thing I already built

The AutoConfig button is superseded. Its only remaining advantage is reloading extensions whose source you can't edit — not your situation. I'd delete `dev-env/firefox/` and `dev-env/bin/firefox-reload-button` rather than keep a monthly-breaking tool around. Nothing was installed into your Firefox, so there's nothing to undo.

column1: # next: can you spawn a fable sugaent and ask them to plan these?

column2:
Confirmed. Here's the report.

## Yes — same architectural fix applies

**Videowall's fix in one sentence:** show the window immediately, do the expensive per-item work (loading a tile) after, off the critical path. **OJ Launcher's `_ready()` does the opposite: it blocks the engine's first frame on synchronous subprocess calls.**

`tools/launcher/launcher.gd:171-200` — `_ready()` runs `_build_ui()`, then calls `_refresh()` and `_self_check()` synchronously, all before returning. `_refresh()` (`launcher.gd:525`) calls `_ojctl(["list", ...])` then `_fetch_history()` calls `_ojctl(["history", ...])` — both go through `OjctlRunner.run()` (`ojctl_runner.gd:24`), which is a **blocking `OS.execute`** on the main thread. That's two Python-interpreter subprocess round-trips (~0.1-0.2s each, measured) serialized on the thread that also has to finish initializing the scene tree and draw the first frame. Nothing appears on screen until both return.

The fix is already half-built in the codebase and just isn't used at startup: `OjctlRunner` has a **threaded async path** (`ojctl_async`/`submit`, `ojctl_runner.gd:45-56`) that `deploy_view.gd` already uses for slower calls (`device`, `plan`, `run`) so a click doesn't freeze the window. The initial `list`/`history` calls in `_refresh()`/`_fetch_history()` never go through it — they use the synchronous static `OjctlRunner.run()` instead, called directly from `_ready()`.

**Mirrors videowall exactly:**
- Videowall: don't fetch/render N tiles before the window is up — show it, mark tiles dormant, populate on demand.
- Launcher: don't block the first frame on two subprocess round-trips — show the window with an empty/loading state, then populate via `_runner.ojctl_async(...)` once ojctl responds.

This won't fix Godot's own engine-init cost (script compilation, GL-compat renderer bring-up) — that's a fixed floor (~0.6-0.7s headless, per the `gd.sh --headless --quit` timing I just ran) and orthogonal to this pattern. But it removes the ~0.2-0.4s of pure subprocess-wait that's currently on the blocking path, and more importantly changes the *felt* launch time: the window paints and becomes interactive immediately instead of sitting blank while Python starts twice.

**Not a fix, worth flagging separately:** `_self_check()` and `_check_fold()` also run synchronously in `_ready()`, but only when `DisplayServer.get_name() == "headless"` — so they don't cost anything in the real windowed launch path. No action needed there.

column2:
There's no single test that says "yes, this is it." It's confirmed two ways: **your pattern matches, and three cheap blood tests come back normal.** That's the whole thing.

## The checklist doctors actually use

There's a published set of criteria for this. It's: heavy sweating in specific spots, for at least 6 months, with no obvious cause — plus **at least two** of the following six:

| | Does it apply to you? |
|---|---|
| Both hands, about the same | ? |
| It gets in the way of daily life | ✅ — the keyboard thing |
| At least once a week | ✅ — constantly |
| Started before you were 25 | ? |
| Someone in the family has it | ❌ — you said no |
| **It stops while you're asleep** | ? |

You need two. You already clearly have two. Fill in the three question marks and you'll likely have four or five, and that's the diagnosis.

## The one to check yourself

**Does it stop when you sleep?** This is the most useful single question, and you can answer it tomorrow morning. When you wake up, before you get out of bed or reach for your phone, notice whether your palms are dry.

Primary hyperhidrosis switches off during sleep — the nerve signal that drives it is tied to being awake. Sweating caused by an illness usually does *not* stop at night. If you wake up with dry hands, that points strongly at the ordinary kind.

Same idea for the other question: **is it only your hands** (plus maybe feet, armpits, face)? Or does your whole body sweat too much? Focused on specific spots = ordinary kind. Everywhere = look for a cause.

## The three blood tests

Ask for these by name at any lab or clinic. All routine, all cheap, no referral needed:

| Test | Turkish name on the form | What it rules out |
|---|---|---|
| Thyroid | **TSH** | Overactive thyroid — the most common real cause of extra sweating |
| Fasting blood sugar | **Açlık kan şekeri** | Diabetes and blood sugar swings |
| Blood count | **Hemogram** (or tam kan sayımı) | Infection, anaemia, and a first look at anything hiding |

Don't eat for 8 hours before, because of the sugar one. If all three come back normal and your pattern fits the checklist, that's your answer. If the thyroid one is off, that changes everything and you treat the thyroid instead.

## What the doctor adds

A dermatologist confirms it mostly by looking and asking — the same questions above, plus checking your palms and feeling your pulse and thyroid. There are two tests you might see mentioned, and neither is for diagnosis:

- **Minor's test (starch-iodine)** — they paint your palm, and the sweating areas turn dark purple. It's used to *map* where to inject before Botox, not to prove you have the condition.
- **Gravimetry** — weighing a paper before and after to measure sweat. Used in research and to track whether treatment is working.

If a clinic wants to run either of these just to tell you that you sweat, they're charging you to confirm something you already know.

## What would change my answer

I'd stop calling it the ordinary kind if any of these turned out to be true:

- It started suddenly in adulthood rather than being lifelong
- Your hands are wet when you wake up
- Your whole body sweats, not just hands and feet
- You're losing weight, having night sweats, or running fevers
- You're taking an antidepressant, opioid, or Alzheimer's medication — those cause it directly

None of those seem to fit from what you've described, which is why I said "almost certainly." Answer the three question marks in the table and check your palms tomorrow morning, and it goes from "almost certainly" to "confirmed enough to treat."

The structural error is that **question 1 lives inside question 4's artifact.** The tripwires — the only thing on the whole site that says what to do — are buried mid-`Karar`, below the inputs card. So the 2-second visit is forced to walk through the 10-minute one.

## Why reading it is expensive right now

**Undifferentiated weight.** A footnote on TEFAS pricing mechanics looks exactly like "TBV lost 1.53 points against TI1 → sell it." The eye cannot triage, so it must *read in order to discover whether it needs to read*. That's the single costliest thing on the site: ~6,700 words per language, nearly all of which must be sampled to find the ~200 that matter today.

**Fourteen columns defeats row-reading.** Under about five columns you read rows. Past that you must pick the column that is your question, scan it vertically, then traverse back. `Fonlarım` scrolls horizontally at 1400px — so you hold fund names in working memory while scrolling right to see their values.

**Bold everywhere kills pop-out.** Salience is pre-attentive only when rare. `markBest` bolds a winner in every group of every table, so the eye gets no free hint and falls back to serial scanning.

**Seven answers to one question force reconciliation.** Seeing "does it beat the deposit" answered seven ways doesn't reassure — it obliges you to check whether the seven agree, and when they differ (different periods, gross vs net, different horizons) to work out why. Involuntary, and the heaviest task on the page.

**Numbers without verdicts transfer the work.** `+3,1 +10,2 +21,3 +46,0 +38,0 1,6 −0,0 0,0 20,77` — you must decide what counts as good. "Fine" is cheaper to read than "20,77".

**Four clocks ticking.** Motion is pre-attentive; it takes attention whether or not it has earned it.

**Collapsibles you must open to know if they're relevant.** "Durum", "İki ayrı karşılaştırma", "Rakamların dışarıda bıraktıkları" — a good collapsible title lets you skip without opening. These don't.

## Four levels

**Level 0 — the main page. One question: is anything wrong?** Default answer is *no*, and saying no is its job. Roughly a screenful, no scroll.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Bugün yapılacak bir şey yok.                  │  ← largest thing on the page
│                                                │
│  1.999.161 ₺    bugün +741 ₺ (+%0,04)          │  ← 3 numbers
│  Sonraki fiyat 17 Eyl Per · vadeli 16 Eki (27g)│  ← the next event, one line
│                                                │
│  ● TI1 politika üstü farkı      −0,39 puan     │
│  ● TBV'nin getirisi             −1,53 puan     │  ← 5 rows, dot + label + reading
│  ● TCMB politika faizi          %37            │
│  ● Bacakların hedeften sapması  ±0,0           │
│  ● 32 günlük vadelinin devri    28 gün         │
│                                                │
│  ▁▂▃▃▄▅▅▆  (değer, 30 gün)                     │  ← one sparkline, no axes
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

~12 numbers and one sentence. About 5% of what the current landing view shows. When a tripwire fires, line 1 becomes the action — "TBV'yi sat, 13:30'a 2 saat" — and turns amber. Nothing else on the screen changes.

**Level 1 — *look*. Seconds.** The holdings table at 6 columns, the calendar, the radar. Plus the deposit answer compressed to **one sentence with one number** and a link down. This is where curiosity is served, not decisions.

**Level 2 — *work*. Minutes, deliberate.** `Karar`: inputs, candidates, the single canonical comparison, cash & timing, mix planner. You come here having decided to spend time.

**Level 3 — *study*. Rare, long.** `Araştırma` + `Yöntem`: fund detail, forecasts, backtests, drivers, the correlation matrix, the optimizer, and all the method prose. Also where `Haber`'s ~80 scored headlines belong — that's a browsing surface, not a dashboard. Its one dashboard-worthy output is a directional observation strong enough to change something, and that surfaces as a single line at level 0.

## The rule that holds it together

**Each level must be answerable without descending, and each summary must be honest enough that you don't feel obliged to audit it.**

The second clause is the demanding one, and it's exactly why the deposit question has to be answered once rather than seven times. A verdict you feel compelled to check is not a verdict — it's just more work with a confident tone.

Which puts the weight on the tripwires. They are the load-bearing idea of the entire site, and they are currently hidden. Everything else — every backtest, every driver decomposition, every forecast band — is evidence *for* them. If they're trustworthy, 95% of visits end in two seconds and the rest of the site is a library you visit on purpose. If they're not, no amount of layout fixes this.

column1: # next: why does it contain declarations? thats such a bad design angle is it not?

column2:
The record of what you *said* you were working on, over time — as opposed to what you did.

`heading.toml` holds declarations: `atlas` is `state = "focus"`, `declared = 2026-08-11`. That's the current one. When you retire atlas and declare something else focus, you edit that entry — and the old fact is gone. Nothing anywhere records that atlas *was* focus from 2026-08-11 until the day you changed it.

Declaration history is keeping those spans:

```
oj      focus    2026-03-02 → 2026-08-11
atlas   focus    2026-08-11 → (still)
moji    parked   2026-09-02 → (still)
```

What it's for: the attention chart shows where your commits actually landed. Declaration history lets me draw the declared-focus span as a band over that same row, so the two are visible together — you said focus here, the work happened there. Ten weeks of focus with a hollow band under it is the picture you can't get any other way.

Without it the chart still answers "what area, since when," just from activity alone. You'd see that atlas went hot in August; you wouldn't see whether that was the plan.

The reason it's a decision now rather than later: activity history already exists in git and can be computed backwards for the whole year whenever you want. Declaration history exists nowhere and starts on the day something begins writing it down.
